title: The Secret Lives of Dentist
full_review:
A taciturn dentist's messy middle-class life loses its moorings when he suspects his wife of infidelity in "The Secret Lives of Dentists" (Manhattan).

Director Alan Rudolph elicits nuanced performances in his mordantly humorous meditation on marital dysfunction, extracting -- pardon the pun -- the truth that, like teeth, married couples' relationships are susceptible to decay.

The at times off-kilter film examines the troubled marriage of two dentists, David Hurst (Campbell Scott), the king of non-confrontation, and his opera-obsessed wife, Dana (Hope Davis). While sharing a successful suburban practice, they have become strangers to each other -- their emotional isolation symbolized by the wall dividing their respective examination rooms. Judiciously inserted flashbacks detail the passion of their courtship and early married life -- including a recurring image of them speeding downhill on a bicycle, denoting the exhilaration of those halcyon days of wine and roses -- but the quotidian demands of career and family have reduced the raging flames of passion to the simmering embers of domesticity.

Stoic to the point of emotional autism, David, at ease playing dentist at his office or dad with his three young daughters, seems incapable of connecting with Dana on any meaningful level -- such intimate probing is reserved for the oral cavities of his patients.

But rot can only be ignored for so long. Inevitably, decay hits a nerve, as happens during a community opera performance, when David spies Dana, who has a small chorus role, sharing an intimate backstage interlude with a faceless stranger. Though his mistrust ferments and his imagination runs wild, he refuses to confront her with his suspicions, afraid of disrupting the equilibrium of their comfortably numb life. He decides to live with uncertainty rather than risk losing the stability he has slaved to achieve. While lacking conclusive proof of any affair, the marriage begins to erode, culminating in a fever-induced third act, when the entire household is struck virulently ill with the flu, allowing the characters' inner turmoil an outward physicality.

Thrown in the delirious mix is one of David's patients, a cantankerous musician named Slater (Denis Leary), who becomes incorporated into the dentist's febrile hallucinations -- sort of a trumpet-playing, cigar-chomping Id -- egging David on and giving voice to his suppressed baser desires.

Adapted from the novel "The Age of Grief" by Jane Smiley, the film paints a darkly humorous, but ultimately compassionate, portrait of married life, comparing it to teeth, observing that both are "permanent but sensitive." Dentistry takes on the mantle of metaphor, as much of the funereal -- at times soporific -- voiceover offers insights from the floss-and-brush school of philosophy, including the film's opening line, "Death is nothing to teeth. life is what destroys teeth." One can only assume that the filmmaker is suggesting that marital disintegration is a slow burn, impervious -- for the most part -- to life's tempestuous tidal waves, but vulnerable to the erosive drip of emotional neglect.

At its core, "The Private Lives of Dentists" is a cautionary tale about the dangers posed to marital health and harmonious home life when the lines of spousal communication break down. Tragically, this often has detrimental effects on not only the couple involved, but other family members as well, especially young children.

Likewise, the film also stresses friendship in marriage as the cornerstone of a loving and committed relationship, a gift shared by spouses long after white-hot sexual passions have cooled.
Due to a brief sexual encounter, sensual fantasy sequences, an instance of same-sex kissing, as well as recurring rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
